tagline.text: Islands guarded by a Spanish fort in the middle of the Sulu Sea

items.credit: National Historical Commission of the Philippines / Public domain / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: More than 40 islands scattered across the Sulu Sea between mainland Palawan and Panay Island, centered on Cuyo, Palawan's oldest town. At the end of a long boat ride, you'll find a 17th-century fort enclosing a church, a sandbar beach that emerges at low tide, hopping between uninhabited islands, and unhurried island village life.

The Cuyo Islands are a group of about 45 islands floating in the Sulu Sea northeast of mainland Palawan, between Panay and Mindoro. Administratively part of Palawan province, they're divided among three municipalities: Cuyo, Magsaysay, and Agutaya. The largest, Cuyo Island, is a volcanic island about 13km long, while many of the smaller islands to the north are low islands formed from uplifted coral reefs, ringed by white sand and shallow jade-colored water.
Cuyo is considered Palawan's oldest town. Augustinian Recollect missionaries began evangelizing here in
, and in

, to guard against Moro pirate raids, they completed a fort whose stone walls — about 10m high and 2m thick — enclose the entire church and monastery. It was the administrative center of the region during the Spanish era, and Cuyonon, the language of the people of Cuyo, was once used almost as a lingua franca across parts of Palawan.

Today, Cuyo town clusters tightly around the fortress church, with a plaza, old wooden houses, and a market close by, while the surrounding sea holds beaches whose sandbars emerge at low tide and scattered small, uninhabited islands. On Pamalican Island to the north sits Amanpulo, a world-class luxury resort, making this an archipelago where the simplest island village and the most expensive getaway coexist side by side.

With almost no fast craft or regular flights, getting here means an overnight boat of more than 12 hours from Iloilo or Puerto Princesa, making it a fit for travelers who enjoy slow travel. It's recommended for those interested in Spanish colonial-era heritage and island culture, or anyone wanting to experience a Filipino island village that hasn't been turned into a tourist attraction.

blocks.title: Cuyo Fort and St. Augustine Church

children.text: A distinctive fort whose coral-stone walls enclose a church, a monastery, and an adoration chapel together. Corner watchtowers and old cannons remain, and the view of the town and sea from atop the walls is excellent.
A beach close to Cuyo port; at low tide, ankle-deep clear water and a wide sandbar stretch far into the distance. It's a good spot for a sunset walk and photos.
Tour Pandan Island, Bisucay Island, Barin Island, and others off Cuyo by bangka, swimming and snorkeling at white sand beaches. Most of these islands are nearly deserted.

Starting from the plaza in front of the fort, walk past Spanish- and American-era wooden houses, the market, and the waterfront. Aside from the sound of tricycles, this is a quiet island town that feels frozen in time.

The highest point on Cuyo Island at about 250m; climb it for a view of Cuyo Island and the small islands scattered across the sea around it. It's best to ask locals for directions and climb in the morning.

blocks.title: A motorbike loop around the island

children.text: Rent a motorbike or tricycle and ride from Cuyo town to the neighboring town of Magsaysay, passing coastal villages and cashew and coconut farms along the way.

blocks.title: The August festival and Ati-Ati dance

children.text: On the feast day of patron saint St. Augustine,
August 28
, dancers paint their faces and bodies black and wear coconut-fiber headdresses for the Ati-Ati dance and street parade.
Cuyo is well known for growing cashews. Roasted cashew nuts and cashew sweets can be bought cheaply at the market, making them good souvenirs.

Depart on the boat to Puerto Princesa or Iloilo

Boats run roughly once a week in each direction, so plan your trip around the arriving and departing boat dates first. Coming from Iloilo and leaving for Puerto Princesa flows naturally into a wider Palawan trip.
Per the 2026 Montenegro Lines schedule, the boat from Iloilo leaves on Saturday at
5 PM
and reaches Cuyo at dawn on Sunday, and the boat back to Iloilo leaves Cuyo on Wednesday at
3 PM

. For a round trip from Iloilo, you'd spend three nights in Cuyo, one day more than this itinerary, which you can use for another island-hopping day or a rest day at Capusan Beach. The boat to Puerto Princesa continues straight on at
2 PM
on the Sunday the boat from Iloilo arrives, so if you come from Iloilo and want to go on to Palawan, you either look around for only half a day or stay a full week until the next week's boat.
Montenegro Lines RORO ferries run the Iloilo–Cuyo–Puerto Princesa route. From Iloilo to Cuyo takes about
12 hours
, with a regular-seat one-way fare of around
; they usually depart in the evening and arrive at dawn.
From Puerto Princesa to Cuyo takes about
15–16 hours
, departing in the afternoon and arriving the next morning. Sailings run roughly once a week in each direction.
Other shipping lines, such as Milagrosa, also operate at times, but sailing days and fares change often depending on weather and the shipping line, so always check the latest timetable.

Most travelers fly from Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), about

There is a Cuyo Airport (CYU) in Magsaysay on Cuyo Island, but the short runway means only small planes can use it, and regular flights are rare or frequently suspended. Check before your trip whether any charter or irregular flights are operating.

Bangkas to nearby islands are hired by negotiating at the pier, with a full-day charter running about

to

is the dry season, and
March–May
, when the sea is calmest, is best for island hopping and the long boat ride. During
December–February

, strong northeast winds can raise swells in the Sulu Sea on some days, occasionally delaying or cancelling boats. On the other hand, these winds draw kitesurfers and windsurfers who come to take advantage of them.
June
to
October

is the wet season, with frequent showers, and when a typhoon crosses central Philippines, passenger ferries can be grounded for days at a time. During this period, missing your return boat could mean staying an extra week, so leave plenty of spare days. The island is liveliest around the St. Augustine feast day on
August 28
, when lodging fills up early.
Even in early
November
, which counts as dry season, a typhoon can pass through. On
November 4, 2025
, Typhoon Tino (Kalmaegi) made landfall at Magsaysay in the Cuyo Islands. If you go in late autumn, be sure to check the PAGASA typhoon forecast before departure.

items.note: Per night, pension to small resort

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Lodging clusters in Cuyo town and Magsaysay. Pensions and small hotels in town run about
a night, while small resorts with a beach or garden run about

. Since boats arrive at dawn, it's worth asking in advance whether early check-in is possible. On Pamalican Island to the north, Amanpulo is an ultra-luxury resort reached by private plane, costing well over a thousand dollars a night, and the island is off-limits to anyone who isn't a guest.
Restaurants are mostly carinderias and small eateries around the plaza in front of the fort and near the market, and a meal costs about

. Grilled fish, seaweed salad, and kinilaw cured in vinegar, all caught offshore, are fresh, and Cuyo-style rice cakes and cashew snacks are worth trying too. Buying roasted cashews at the market makes a versatile snack for island hopping and a good souvenir. Restaurants close early, so it's best to eat dinner early.
Set your travel dates around the boat schedule. Confirm the arriving and departing boats first, then book your lodging.
The air-conditioned section of the overnight boat gets cold, so bring long clothing and a blanket, and keep valuables on your person.
Card payment is rarely accepted and ATMs aren't reliable, so bring all the cash you'll need for your stay from Iloilo or Puerto Princesa.
The Capsan Beach sandbar is widest at low tide, so check the tide schedule before you go.
Snorkel gear is hard to rent locally. Bring your own or ask your lodging in advance.
The fortress church is an active parish with Mass, so wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees, and it's best to avoid sightseeing during Mass times.
Cell signal is available in town but the internet tends to be slow, so save the boat schedule and your lodging's contact info in advance.

Passenger ferries to and from Cuyo run only about once a week in each direction and are often cancelled due to weather. Missing your return boat can strand you for days to a week, so book flights with plenty of buffer and be sure to check the shipping line's latest notices.
The island has no major hospital, making it hard to handle emergencies. Bring plenty of basic medicine and any personal medication.
When crossing between islands on a small bangka, wear a life jacket, and it's safer to postpone departure on windy days.
The tide comes in quickly over the sandbar, so if you've walked far out, watch the tide and head back early.
Privately owned islands like Pamalican cannot be landed on without permission. Check with your boatman during island hopping.
Don't touch coral or marine life, and don't leave trash on the islands.
